answer_1.quote: Generalizing seamlessly to (seemingly) arbitrary language understanding, reasoning, and generation tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) have arguably become the first ubiquitously adopted language technology, with application ranging from search engines, interactive agents and knowledge retrieval to various content generation tasks.
answer_1.outputs: LLM-generated answers to knowledge-intensive questions in 30 languages

answer_2.quote: We use MFAVA to estimate HD model's per-language performances (precision and recall).

answer_3.quote: We synthesize a silver multilingual hallucination evaluation dataset by prompting a state-of-the-art LLM (GPT-4) to introduce hallucinations in its answers to knowledge-seeking questions

answer_4.quote: We source the annotations via Prolific, recruiting 5 annotators per language: all five annotators first annotated the same 50 instances, after which they were given non-overlapping sets of 50 more instances.
answer_4.guideline: Annotators were provided the reference Wikipedia page and the (hallucination-enriched) generation from MFAVA-Silver (without GPT-4's hallucination annotations) and asked to label hallucinated spans. They also rated the likelihood of hallucination fooling a human reader on a 5-degree Likert scale.
criteria: fine-grained hallucination type (e.g., entity, relation, invented, contradictory, unverifiable, subjective)
likelihood of fooling a human reader
